INTRODUCTION
KASPEREK AND ZEBROWSKI (1971) and Lhermitte et al. (1973) have described
a progressive disorder, characterized by a striking, tonically maintained rigidity
of the trunk and limbs, and by painful spasms evoked by sensory or emotional
stimuli. In the 2 cases described in those reports there were other neurological
signs, including peripheral sensory impairment, signs of brain-stem dysfunction
and abnormalities in the CSF. At autopsy there were changes in the spinal cord
and lower brain-stem consistent with an active encephalomyelitis. Kasperek and
Zebrowski (1971) suggested that their case could be classified as an example of
'stiff man syndrome' (Moersch and Woltmann, 1956; Gordon et al., 1967) but
Lhermitte et al. (1973) preferred to regard both Kasperek and Zebrowski's case
and their own as a new entity. They compared the rigidity in these 2 patients to
that previously described with central spinal cord lesions in man by Penry et al.
(1960), by Rushworth et al. (1961), and by earlier authors. This form of rigidity of
spinal origin has also been studied experimentally, notably by Gelfan and Tarlov
(1959).
We have studied 2 patients with the syndrome of subacute encephalomyelitis
with rigidity as described by Kasperek and Zebrowski (1971) and by Lhermitte
et al. (1973). In both the brunt of the pathological process fell on the cervical cord.
In our second case the course was much more rapid and the clinical features were
similar to the 3 patients described by Campbell and Garland (1956) under the
designation 'subacute myoclonic spinal neuronitis.' We shall discuss the possible
interrelationships between these and other similar disorders in this report.

Case 1. A 61-year-old woman was admitted to another hospital in May 1973 for investigation of
stiffness of her legs and difficulty in walking of about four weeks' duration. She also complained of
shaking of her legs from time to time, and of precipitancy of micturition. Her gait was described as
slow and clumsy but she improved with physiotherapy and was discharged after a few days. She was

28 A. M. WHITELEY, M. SWASH AND H. URICH
readmitted in July 1973 because her gait had become more unsteady, and she had fallen several times. On
examination she was alert and orientated, but she could walk only a few shuffling steps with assistance
from two nurses. It was thought that there was no weakness but muscle tone was increased in all limbs,
and the reflexes were brisk. The plantar responses were flexor. There was a coarse, irregular tremor of
both hands. Sensation was normal. She did not improve with physiotherapy and took her own.
discharge a few days later.
In November 1973 she was admitted to The London Hospital after a fall from her chair at home.
For several months she had been able to walk only one or two steps. Her mental condition remained
unimpaired. Her speech was quiet and slightly slurred, but the cranial nerves and visual fields were
normal on formal testing. The fundi were normal. She could sit in an armchair and could feed herself
slowly and read a newspaper, but she could barely stand without assistance, and she could not sit up
in bed unaided. She was doubly incontinent.
There was persistent, maintained contraction of all muscle groups, except those of the face. There
was a striking poverty of spontaneous movement of the limbs, but not of the face. The upper limbs were
held adducted and flexed against the chest wall, but the wrists and ringers were hyperextended. The
legs were maintained partially flexed at hips and knees and there was pronounced plantar flexion of feet
and toes. The spine was rigid and held in an exaggerated lordosis and the abdominal musculature was
also tonically contracted. All the contracted muscles felt hard. These postures were maintained plastically
against resistance and there was no clasp-knife phenomenon or cogwheel element on passive stretch.
The lengthening and shortening reactions were absent and rotational movements of the neck did not
change the posture. However, all attempts to manipulate the limbs passively provoked intense muscular
spasm, beginning in the limb examined and slowly spreading to all muscle groups. On cessation of
manipulation the spasm gradually lessened over the course of several minutes, so that the increased
resting tone and the postural abnormality again became apparent. Other stimuli, such as a sudden
noise, prolonged questioning, emotional distress; a full bladder, or cutaneous stimuli during neuro-
logical examination, also provoked painful spasms, which prevented all voluntary movement. They
were usually accompanied by generalized sweating and the patient feared examination because of
them. They were also provoked by voluntary movement, and if one occurred while the patient was
sitting or standing unsupported she would fall. The pattern of muscular activity in these spasms, and
its time course, was unlike that of ordinary flexor or extensor spasms. The tendon reflexes were brisk,
but there was no clonus and both plantar responses were flexor. There was no tremor, fasciculation or
wasting. Sensation was normal. The general examination was normal.
Investigations. Routine haematological and biochemical investigations were normal. Radiographs of
the skull, cervical spine and chest were normal. The electroencephalogram showed only a mild non-
specific slowing of background activity. The CSF was clear and colourless. It contained 40 mg dl
protein (IgG 15 per cent) and 14 leucocytes/c.mm (90 per cent polymorphs and 10 per cent lymphocytes).
The Wassermann reaction was negative in blood and CSF. Electromyography was not performed.
Progress. She was transferred to another hospital where she died thirteen months after the onset of
her illness. During this time she gradually became more rigid and immobile. Treatment with levodopa,
orphenadrine, diazepam, baclofen and dimethothiazine had no effect on her rigidity. Terminally,
although alert and orientated and able to speak quietly and slowly, the legs were rigidly extended with
the feet plantar-flexed and the arms maintained in a posture of mild triple flexion. There was no voluntary
movement. The posture did not vary when she was turned from side to side and it could not be over-
come by force. Sensation remained normal.
Post-mortem examination (PM 19/A/74). There was widespread broncho-
pneumonia. Bilateral pyelonephritis, a benign ovarian cyst and a small benign
thyroid nodule were also found. A thorough search failed to reveal a malignant
neoplasm. The muscles appeared normal.

cases.text:
Case 2. A healthy 19-year-old man complained of an aching pain in his back and legs. Within nine
days of the onset of this symptom he noticed weakness of his legs and difficulty in walking. In addition,
he began to experience brief attacks of rigidity and jerking of his limbs, often apparently provoked by
sensory stimuli. Thirteen days after the onset of his illness he could walk only with support, the attacks
of rigidity and jerking of the trunk and limbs were more severe and more frequent, his speech was
slurred and his swallowing was impaired.
He was admitted to another hospital where he was observed for a week. During this time he was
conscious and orientated. A mild remittent fever was noted. It was thought that his symptoms were not
due to organic disease and he was discharged. At home that evening he became unable to stand and was
taken by a friend to a different hospital where it was also considered that his complaints were not due
to organic disease. Next morning, twenty-one days after the onset of his illness, he was found dead on
the floor beside his bed.
Post-mortem examination (Coroner's PM 37/A/74). The only macroscopic
abnormality was pulmonary congestion. No virus was isolated from post-mortem
samples of liver, muscle, blood or faeces. Blood complement-fixation titres, against
influenza A, Sendai, adenovirus, Coxiella burneti, psittacosis, Mycoplasma
pneumonia, mumps, herpes simplex, varicella zoster and Coxsackie types B,, B3,
B4, B5 and B6 viruses were within normal limits, but the titres against measles and
Coxsackie B2 viruses were slightly raised (1:160). No drugs were detected in blood,
urine or gastric contents.
Central nervous system. The macroscopic appearances of brain, spinal cord and
meninges were normal. Sections of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded material
were stained with hsmatoxylin and eosin, with luxol fast blue, and by Holzer's
and by Glees and Marsland's methods.
Spinal cord: the cord showed lymphocytic cuffing of vessels, increased numbers
of rod-shaped microglial cells, and gliosis of the central grey matter. Neuronal loss
was inconspicuous, but there were several figures of neuronophagia around
degenerating nerve cells, both large and small. No selective loss of any particular
cell type was observed. There were no definite changes in the White matter. Scanty
inflammatory cells were seen in the meninges.
Brain-stem: the inflammatory response continued cephalad from the spinal
cord as far as the upper mesencephalon. Microglial proliferation was most marked
in the lower medulla and in the pontine tegmentum, in which the inferior and
superior olivary nuclei (fig. 6) and the periaqueductal regions were particularly
affected. The substantia nigra was also involved. Astrocytic gliosis was prominent
in the medullary reticular formation, the floor of the fourth ventricle and the
periaqueductal region. Neuronal loss was evident in the inferior olivary nuclei
and in the substantia nigra. Ascending and descending tracts were normal.

FIG. 6 (Case 2). Inferior olive. Haimatoxylin and eosin. x 140. Loss of neurons and increased numbers of
microglial cells.
Basal ganglia and thalamus: there was a mild, diffuse microgliosis.
Cerebellum: no definite abnormalities were found.
Cerebral cortex: a thin, patchily distributed perivascular lymphocytic cuffing
was seen. There was a minimal microglial proliferation. Oligodendroglial
satellitosis was present in the deeper cortical layers and a scanty meningeal cellular
reaction was evident.
DISCUSSION
The predominant clinical feature in both our patients was rigidity with muscular
spasms but the course differed in the two cases. In Case 1 there was a progressive
illness of thirteen months' duration. Rigidity and slowly developing muscular
spasms, with some recurrent bodily jerking, and with loss of orientating and
postural reflexes were the main features, and these made assessment of voluntary
power difficult. There was a slight lymphocytosis in the cerebrospinal fluid. The
reflexes were normal and there was no sensory abnormality. Intellect was preserved.
No diagnosis was established in life and, indeed, in the first few months of her
illness most observers thought that her symptoms were hysterical. Our second
patient died after a very much more rapidly progressive illness. Rigidity and
muscular spasms were the only recorded abnormality and even on the evening of
his death it was not thought that he was suffering from an organic disease. There
is no evidence that there was a sensory abnormality or that the reflexes and plantar
responses were abnormal, but the available clinical information about this case
is scanty.

34 A. M. WHITELEY, M. SWASH AND H. URICH
The clinical and pathological features of our Case 1 are similar to those of the
two patients described in the reports of Kasperek and Zebrowski (1971) and of
Lhermitte et al. (1973).
Kasperek and Zebrowski (1971) described a 49-year-old woman, whose illness
began with radicular pains and a distal sensory disturbance in both legs. During
a period of seven months she gradually developed weakness of her limbs, and
slight sensory impairment in a glove and stocking distribution. During the two
months before admission she had noticed increasing stiffness of both arms and
of her left leg. The stiffness was often induced, like a spasm, by touch, passive
movement of a limb, or by a sudden sound and it was usually accompanied by
pain and sweating. On examination the arms were rigid and maintained in a posture
similar to that of decerebration. The left leg was stiffly extended during her frequent
painful spasms. Resting tone in the legs was reduced. The tendon reflexes were all
absent and the plantar responses were both flexor. She deteriorated and developed
impairment of conjugate gaze to the left with vertical nystagmus. The spasms
intensified and also involved her face, but there was a slight improvement with
oral diazepam. The cerebrospinal fluid protein content was slightly increased.
Electromyographic studies showed persistent, normal motor-unit activity at rest,
which was enhanced during a spasm. A few weeks before she died, seventeen
months after the onset of her illness, the spasms ceased to involve the legs which
then remained hypotonic and areflexic.
At autopsy there was no macroscopic abnormality but microscopy showed an
encephalomyelitis restricted to the spinal cord, brain-stem and left hippocampal
region. Perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, gliosis and neuronal loss were most
marked in the cervical cord, medulla and pons. In the cord there was diffuse
neuronal loss particularly evident in the medial part of the anterior horns, in the
posterior horns and in Clarke's column. White-matter degeneration was seen
mainly in the posterior columns, dorsal spinocerebellar tracts, medial longitudinal
fasciculus, medial lemnisci and in the inferior cerebellar peduncles. The vestibular
nuclei, dorsal cochlear nuclei, gracile and cuneate nuclei, reticular formation,
spinal trigeminal nuclei and abducens nuclei were also slightly involved. The
posterior root ganglia were not examined.
Lhermitte et al. (1973) reported a man aged 71 years at death, who gradually
developed difficulty in walking, with stiffness of his legs, and clumsiness of his
hands. When examined three months later resting tone was markedly increased in
the legs. The tendon reflexes were increased and the plantar responses were extensor.
Joint position sense was impaired in all limbs. A myelogram was normal but the
cerebrospinal fluid contained 60 mg protein/dl and 60 lymphocytes/c.mm. He
gradually deteriorated. A year later the legs were held in a posture of maintained
partial extension and he could no longer stand. The arms were weak but hypotonic.
The reflexes were brisk in the legs but diminished in the arms. A convergent
strabismus had appeared. Spasms, usually provoked by cutaneous stimuli but
accompanied by increasingly severe rigidity at rest, developed and particularly

PROGRESSIVE ENCEPHALOMYELITIS WITH RIGIDITY 35
affected the trunk, legs, neck and jaw, but not the arms. These were relieved, to
some extent, by diazepam and by baclofen. Electromyographic examination of the
legs showed persistent activity of normal motor units, with increased activity
when the limbs were touched or moved, and during spasms. He died thirty-eight
months after the onset of his illness.
At autopsy microscopical examination showed an encephalomyelitis confined
to the brain-stem and spinal cord. There was marked neuronal loss in the spinal
cord, especially in the cervical anterior horns. In the white matter there was
degeneration of the dorsal columns and, to a lesser degree, of the anterior spino-
thalamic tracts. In the brain-stem the oculomotor and abducens nuclei, and the
reticular formation were affected. Perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and gliosis
were prominent in the cervical cord and medulla. The posterior root ganglia were
not examined.
In these 2 cases and in our Case 1 there was a steadily progressive, incapacitating
illness characterized by sustained muscular rigidity and by spasms. The rigidity
was present in both trunk and limbs and was associated with impaired voluntary
movement and with an abnormal posture. Intense painful spasms occurred
spontaneously and were also initiated by various stimuli, including light touch,
passive and active limb movement and sudden sounds. The spasms developed over
several seconds, spread to involve adjacent muscle groups, and persisted for several
minutes. They were accompanied by profuse sweating. In the 2 previous cases
there was slight distal sensory impairment but this was not found in our patient.
Brain-stem signs were evident in 2 of the 3 patients but consciousness was preserved
in all of them.
The neuropathological findings consisted of perivascular lymphocytic cuffing,
increased microglial activity, astrocytic gliosis and neuronal loss, which mainly
affected the spinal cord, especially in the cervical region, and the brain-stem. In
the case reported by Lhermitte et al. (1973) an almost complete loss of anterior
horn cells in the cervical region could be correlated with flaccidity, fasciculation
and areflexia in the arms. In Kasperek and Zebrowski's (1971) case the legs became
flaccid a few weeks before death and this was attributed to the severe involvement
of the posterior columns in the lumbar region in this case. In all 3 cases there was
a severe tract degeneration in the spinal cord but the pattern of involvement
varied. The only constant feature was preservation of the corticospinal tracts. In
the 2 previously reported cases the posterior columns were virtually destroyed but
in our case the posterior columns were conspicuously preserved, with the cortico-
spinal tracts, although there was extensive destruction of the remainder of the
white matter of the spinal cord. The dorsal root ganglia were not examined in the
2 previous cases, but were normal in our patient. The dorsal spinocerebellar tracts
and Clarke's column were involved in Kasperek and Zebrowski's (1971) case and
in our Case 1, but not in the patient described by Lhermitte et al. (1973). The
pattern of abnormality in the brain-stem was inconstant. Tract degeneration
in the brain-stem could be followed from the spinal cord. In each case nuclear

36 A. M. WHITELEY, M. SWASH AND H. URICH
involvement included the abducens nuclei and the reticular formation, but
other nuclei were also affected. The cerebellum and basal ganglia were always
unaffected, and the cerebral cortex was involved only in one case (Kasperek and
Zebrowski, 1971).
The clinical and pathological findings in these 3 cases are so similar that it
seems likely they suffered from a similar disorder, consisting of a slowly
progressive ascending inflammatory process leading to death from brain-stem
involvement. Both Kasperek and Zebrowski (1971) and Lhermitte et al. (1973) have
suggested that a viral infection might be responsible but there is no evidence, other
than the pathological appearances, to confirm or refute this suggestion.
Our Case 2 suffered from a more rapidly progressive disorder than these patients
but, like them, rigidity provoked by various sensory stimuli was the major
manifestation. The neuropathological findings were also similar, but there was no
tract degeneration, perhaps because the patient survived for only three weeks.
Campbell and Garland (1956) described 3 patients, 2 of whom died, in whom a
similar illness occurred, which they termed 'subacute myoclonic spinal neuronitis.'
The illness in these patients began with fever and painful muscular spasms, which
were evoked by any cutaneous stimulus. The spasms principally affected legs and
trunk and in one case they were so severe that curare and spinal anaesthesia were
needed to control them. In their third patient, who survived for a month after the
onset, a flaccid paraplegia supervened terminally but no other neurological
abnormalities were noted in any of the 3 patients. The cerebrospinal fluid was
normal in the 2 patients in whom it was examined. One recovered in a few days but
the other 2 died and, at autopsy, there was an inflammatory myelitis limited to the
grey matter of the cord, principally affecting the lumbar and cervical regions. There
was pronounced perivascular lymphocytic cuffing, neuronal loss, neuronophagia
and microgliosis. The white matter appeared normal. Campbell and Garland
(1956) noted that 2 of their 3 cases had been treated with radiotherapy a short time
before the onset of the illness and suggested that this might have been an aetiological
factor. There was no history of exposure to ionizing radiation in either of our
2 patients but the histological findings in our Case 2 were very similar to those
found by Campbell and Garland (1956), although the brain-stem was more
prominently involved. The significance of the slightly raised complement-
fixation titres to measles and to Coxsackie B2 viruses in our case is uncertain.
Encephalomyelitis as a cause of rigidity is well recognized, but uncommon.
Campbell and Garland (1956) were impressed, for example, with the clinical and
pathological similarity between their cases and the spinal form of encephalitis
lethargica (Ellis, 1920; von Economo, 1931), and in this disorder, as in one of their
cases, flaccid paralysis was said to supervene after spasms and myoclonus had
ceased (Walshe, 1920). Swanson et al. (1962) observed both rigidity and myoclonus
in a group of patients with acute generalized encephalomyelitis but coma was
almost invariable and there were extensive cortical lesions at autopsy. Stimulus-
sensitive myoclonus, without rigidity, occurred in a patient described by Hopkins
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/brain/article/99/1/27/256306 by University of Calgary user on 09 May 2023
PROGRESSIVE ENCEPHALOMYELITIS WITH RIGIDITY 37
and Michael (1974). The CSF showed abnormalities consistent with an
inflammatory process and electrophysiological studies suggested a lesion located
in the spinal cord. Recovery was complete. Silfverskiold (1962) described 3 girls
in whom segmental myoclonus was attributed to viral encephalomyelitis.
The pathophysiology of rigidity occurring with spinal lesions is poorly
understood. This phenomenon has been described in various cord lesions,
including trauma to the cervical spine (Thorbura, 1887), cervical syringomyelia
(Babinski, 1913), cervical subacute necrotizing myelopathy (Penry et al., 1960) and
astrocytoma of the cervical spinal cord (Rushworth et al., 1961). In all these cases
some anterior horn cells remained, although there was extensive destruction of
white matter and of the central and posterior parts of the grey matter, and it was
suggested that the maintained plastic rigidity was due to a continuous spontaneous
discharge of these isolated anterior horn cells ('alpha rigidity')- Gelfan and Tarlov
(1959) observed a similar rigidity in the dog, after ischaemic lesions had been
produced in the central grey matter by aortic ligation, and found that it could be
abolished only by anaesthesia, or by anterior root section. Penry et al. (1960) and
Rushworth et al. (1961) suggested that Renshaw cell inhibition might be impaired
in their cases. Although, in the cat, it has been shown that the Renshaw cells are
located in the medial part of the anterior horn, in Rexed's lamina VI1 (Thomas
and Wilson, 1965), their location in man is unknown. It is perhaps worth noting,
none the less, that in Case 2 of Penry et al. (I960), and in our Case 1, anterior horn
cell loss was particularly prominent medially. In our cases, and in those of Kasperek
and Zebrowski (1971) and Lhermitte et al. (1973), there were also lesions in the
brain-stem but these were not extensive and their location was such that it appears
unlikely that the rigidity and spasm from which these patients suffered could have
been due to brain-stem disease. Furthermore, the clinical features of the rigidity
were unlike spasticity with flexor or extensor spasms, extrapyramidal rigidity,
decerebration or decortication. Tonic muscular spasms have also been observed
in patients with multiple sclerosis, and Osterman and Westerberg (1975) have
suggested that these might be due to transversely spreading ephaptic activation of
axons within a partially demyelinated lesion in fibre tracts in the central nervous
system. Such a mechanism could also be a factor in other disorders in which
myelinated fibre tracts have been damaged, and one of Osterman and Westerberg's
(1975) patients had a traumatic cervical myelopathy.
In our cases purely muscular disorders, such as polymyositis, were excluded on
clinical grounds and there was no evidence of a coincidental metabolic cause for
the rigidity, such as hyponatraemia. The syndrome of continuous muscle-fibre
activity described by Isaacs (1961) can also be excluded by the clinical and neuro-
pathological findings. In considering the differential diagnosis of their case
Kasperek and Zebrowski (1971) suggested that the signs were consistent with
a diagnosis of 'stiff man syndrome' (Moersch and Woltmann, 1956). However,
their patient had other clinical abnormalities, including sensory loss, brain-stem
signs and an abnormal cerebrospinal fluid, which according to the criteria of
Downloaded from https://academic.oup.com/brain/article/99/1/27/256306 by University of Calgary user on 09 May 2023
38 A. M. WHITELEY, M. SWASH AND H. URICH
Gordon et al. (1967) exclude this diagnosis. Lhermitte et al. (1973) also took this
view and suggested that their own case, and that of Kasperek and Zebrowski
(1971), represented a unique form of viral encephalomyelitis, which predominantly
affected the spinal cord. Further, they regarded the neuropathological findings in
the 2 patients as inconsistent with a diagnosis of stiff man syndrome.
The stiff man syndrome (Moersch and Woltmann, 1956) is a disorder
characterized by the gradual development of symmetrical rigidity of axial and
proximal limb muscles. Typically this rigidity is associated with spasms of
intensified muscular contraction, evoked by sensory or emotional stimuli. The illness
begins with aching and stiffness of axial muscles, which spreads to the proximal
limb muscles in a period of several weeks or months. The rigidity itself consists of
a board-like contraction of affected muscles which may lessen during sleep, or
with diazepam therapy. There are no other neurological signs and the CSF is
normal. Other causes of muscular rigidity, such as metabolic disorders, poly-
myositis or chronic tetanus (McQuillen et al., 1967) must be excluded. Gordon
et al. (1967) reviewed all the cases published before 1966 and found 44 cases which,
they believed, were acceptable examples of this syndrome. We have ourselves been
able to accept only 35 cases in the literature up to 1974, in which all the other
possible causes of sustained muscular rigidity had been excluded (Table 1). We
have thus excluded several of the cases accepted by Gordon et al. (1967). Of these
35 cases, 29 were alive at the time of their report. Fourteen of them were reported
by Moersch and Woltmann (1956) but only one of these was fully described
and in another the authors state that there were sensory symptoms. It is possible,
therefore, that the diagnosis might also be challenged in some of these patients.
Seventeen of the reported cases were followed for more than four years and when
last examined were leading active lives. Eight patients died and 6 of these had
been followed for more than four years. In these the disease was said to have
progressed in the year before death.
Post-mortem examinations have been reported in only 4 cases. In one, of more
than fifteen years' duration, no details were recorded (Asher, 1958) and in 2, both
of more than four years' duration, the brain was said to be normal but the spinal
cord was not examined (Moersch and Woltmann, 1956; Cohen, 1966). The only
detailed examination of the central nervous system is that of a 76-year-old woman,
described by Trethowan et al. (I960), who had had rigidity and spasms of the trunk
and legs, with normal sensation, for four years. The arms were normal. The
cerebrospinal fluid was not examined. At autopsy the spinal cord showed slight
pallor of the posterior columns, some loss of Nissl substance and pyknosis of
anterior horn cells, and an excess of lipofuscin pigment. In the brain there were
neurofibrillary tangles and senile plaques, and the white matter was generally
paler than normal. These changes were attributed to ageing. It is apparent that
more pathological data are required from some of the previously reported cases
of 'stiff man syndrome' before the nosological position of this syndrome can be
adequately assessed.

For the present we concur with the conclusion of Lhermitte et al. (1973) that
the clinical features in their case, and that of Kasperek and Zebrowski (1971) are
sufficiently characteristic to suggest that these patients, and our Case 1, were
suffering from a rare but distinctive disorder, different from the ill-defined 'stiff
man syndrome,' and from other examples of rigidity due to spinal cord or brain-
stem disease. It is possible that similar cases may have occurred at the time of the
epidemic of encephalitis lethargica (Ellis, 1920).
The relation of subacute myoclonic spinal neuronitis (Campbell and Garland,
1956) to this syndrome of progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity is uncertain.
Although the clinical course in these patients, as in our Case 2, was short the signs
were similar and the pathological findings were also those of a meningo-
encephalomyelitis, principally located in the upper spinal cord. In all these cases
the illness was very short and this may account for the relatively sparse changes
in the white matter of the cord. We consider that it is possible that this subacute
disorder is a more rapidly progressive form of the disease first described by Kasperek
and Zebrowski (1971) of which our Case 1 is an example.
SUMMARY
Two cases of encephalomyelitis are described in which the major clinical
manifestation was muscular rigidity and stimulus-sensitive muscular spasms. It
is suggested, from pathological evidence, that this rigidity was of spinal origin,
and that this disorder is a rare but recognizable entity. Comparison is made with
previously reported cases of rigidity of spinal origin, including encephalitis
lethargica, and with 'subacute myoclonic spinal neuronitis' and the 'stiff man
syndrome.'
